title: 'No comment': York police union hires former cop who struck, killed teen while driving
article: The York Regional Police Association has hired former police officer and convicted criminal Remo Romano as a peer support worker in a controversial move that's certain to upset some.

The decision to install Romano, from Woodbridge, in the newly created role for which he had little or no training, comes soon after he was released from his eight-month jail sentence and has rankled some members of the police fraternity.

"The public is demanding more accountability of police than ever before and associations/services need to remember the old adage: 'It is not what you do, but what you appear to have done'," wrote former YRPA secretary treasurer Phil Shrewsbury-Gee in an email to yorkregion.com .
However, one current member of York Regional Police said given the circumstances, she believes it's the right move.

"This is a nice guy who was coming to work who made a mistake, there was no malicious intent," the individual said. "I think there's a difference between someone who behaves like a cowboy and someone who is genuinely trying to do his job and unfortunately something terrible occurs."
For its part, the YRPA said it had "no comment" on the matter.
The Romano story dates back almost a decade to February 2014, when the then Det. Const. was part of a covert operation to locate perfume thieves.
At some point Romano fell behind the rest.
Driving at 115 km/h on St. Clair Avenue East to catch up to his colleagues who were following an individual they believed to be a suspect, Romano hit and killed Carla Abogado.
The 18-year-old, who was jaywalking to get to her home, died on impact, which left the F-150 pick-up he was driving badly damaged, showing the force of the impact.
The first of three contentious trials, lasting almost five years, ended in a mistrial.
In the second, Romano was acquitted.
However, in the third trial, granted because of a successful Crown appeal, he was found guilty of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing death resulting in his jailing.
As a result he was fired from York Regional Police in accordance with the Police Services Act, which allows officers to have a criminal record, but does not allow a member to be incarcerated.

Shrewsbury-Gee insisted that police who show preferential or beneficial treatment to one of their own because that person was an officer when the offence was committed are doing a disservice to police everywhere.

"For police personnel, it is very important that the public can trust that the poor or malicious conduct by police officers be investigated fully and fairly, and the resulting prosecution and accountability follow that same path," he added.
The aforementioned police officer disagrees, insisting not only would the public be fine with the move, but the police fraternity are also in support.
She said this is obvious given the number of York officers, many of whom are high ranking, who donated to his GoFundMe page with their names attached to their donations.

"I think the public would say he was in the right place at the right time," the person added. "He was at work, acting in good faith, it was four lanes and not residential. I wouldn't say it was reckless."
The officer further suggested that Romano was forced to go through three trials because he was a police officer, insisting a member of the public would never face this treatment.
"Remo Romano is one of the kindest, most humblest gentle men in the world," said the officer, who added that he's a father of five.
The Abogado family, who lost their daughter and were also forced to go through the agonizing court process, did not reply to attempts to reach them.
